questions.question: Using Mokoena Backpack Works' budget — selling price R120, variable costs R64 per bag, fixed costs R560 000, planned output 20 000 bags — build the four-line contribution statement and explain why contribution is not profit.
questions.expected_answer: Sales: 20 000 bags at R120 — R2 400 000. Less total variable costs: 20 000 at R64 — R1 280 000, made up of direct materials R34, direct labour R22 and selling and distribution R8 per bag. Total contribution: R1 120 000, confirmed as 20 000 times the R56 contribution per unit. Less fixed costs of R560 000 — factory overheads R356 000 plus administration R204 000. Budgeted profit: R560 000. Contribution is not profit because each bag's R56 must first pay toward the wall of fixed costs, which stands regardless of output; until total contribution covers R560 000 the business as a whole is still in loss, and only after that point does each bag's R56 drop through as pure profit. Variable costs are constant per unit but grow in total with output; fixed costs are constant in total but shrink per unit as volume spreads them — which is why a full unit cost is only true at the output it was calculated for.

questions.question: Calculate Mokoena's break-even point in units and in rand, interpret it against the plan, and state the rounding rule with its reason.
questions.expected_answer: Break-even units: total fixed costs over contribution per unit — R560 000 over R56 — 10 000 bags. Break-even value: 10 000 at R120 — R1 200 000. Check: revenue R1 200 000 less variable costs of R640 000 gives contribution of exactly R560 000, equal to fixed costs, so profit is zero. Interpretation: the survival line sits at exactly half the planned 20 000 bags, so the budget carries a margin of safety of 10 000 bags — 50 percent — and the bags beyond break-even deliver R56 each, producing the budgeted profit of R560 000. Rounding: when the division is not exact, always round UP — at R560 100 of fixed costs the division gives 10 001 comma 8, and at 10 001 bags a sliver of loss remains, so break-even is only reached at 10 002. Break-even is a threshold: the wall is either paid or it is not.

questions.question: Test three changes on the break-even point — price cut to R112, canvas up R4 per bag, fixed costs up R56 000 — and name the model's assumptions.
questions.expected_answer: Price cut to R112: contribution falls to R48, and R560 000 over R48 gives 11 666 comma 7, so break-even rises to 11 667 bags — an R8 cut moves the line by 1 667 bags because price cuts land directly on the contribution. Canvas up R4: variable cost R68, contribution R52, break-even R560 000 over R52 — 10 769 comma 2, so 10 770 bags. Fixed costs up R56 000: the wall becomes R616 000 over the unchanged R56 — exactly 11 000 bags. The two routes differ: variable increases shrink each unit's contribution; fixed increases grow the wall to be paid — either way the margin of safety thins, and the tool prices each decision before it is signed. Assumptions: selling price and unit variable cost constant at any volume, fixed costs that never step, and everything made is sold — approximately true near the planned range, weaker far outside it, where fixed costs step, bulk discounts bend variable costs, and prices may need to fall to move extreme volumes.
